audience.programmeDescription: History at Erasmus studies social, cultural, economic and political change from 1500, with particular attention to the last two centuries and questions about society today. Students learn to work with historical sources, choose a focus area and complete a thesis. This comparison shows Economic History with a minor and a field-specific internship. The degree is the Dutch History track: lectures are English, first-year practicals are Dutch, and later teaching and assessment can use both languages under the programme rules.
audience.comparisonExplanation: Each UCR option combines all six available History courses with a different set of supporting fields. The closest option adds economics, social analysis, art history and historiography; the other options emphasise international order or social and cultural representation. These are substantial interdisciplinary historical programmes with different scope from a full History degree. They do not reproduce Erasmus’s complete economic-history focus area, required individual thesis or internship. A shared row means a meaningful partial relationship; blank cells identify other content or a gap.

curriculum.limitation: This is one permitted route. Erasmus also offers other focus areas and third-year choices. The elective and minor subjects remain open within the programme’s approved options.

componentNotes.y2-elective: One 7.5-EC course from the programme’s approved elective options.
componentNotes.y3-thesis-class: Thesis preparation within the selected Economic History focus area; entry requires the completed first year and sufficient second/third-year and focus-area credits.
componentNotes.y3-thesis: Compulsory individual 15-EC historical research thesis; the thesis class must be passed before submission.
componentNotes.y3-minor: 15 EC chosen from the applicable minor admission matrix.
componentNotes.y3-internship: Field-specific 15-EC internship; the first year must be completed. The programme alternatively permits two electives worth 15 EC.

cellNotes.text: Researching the American Century develops historical questions, critical engagement with sources and a substantial research paper. It does not guarantee the former Walcheren Expedition archive topic or replace Erasmus’s independent Economic History thesis.

concepts.label: History, economy & society
concepts.concept: A historically anchored programme combines all six available UCR History courses with three art-history courses on Renaissance-to-modern visual culture, early-modern global connections and historiography. Economics, sociology, political thought and international relations supply complementary explanations of institutions, inequality and change; quantitative and qualitative methods support inquiry. The final History seminar researches primary sources from the 1809 Walcheren Expedition. This is sustained historical study, but it does not reproduce Erasmus’s complete economic-history focus area, philosophy-of-history course, individual thesis or internship.

concepts.label: History, international relations & conflict
concepts.concept: A historical programme centres all six UCR History courses, with historically grounded work on human rights, political thought and race in media. International-relations theory, comparative politics, peace and conflict, international and EU law, EU politics and social theory provide complementary tools for studying international order and power. The six-course History sequence and historical-source research supply the historical anchor; the law and politics courses do not become specialised diplomatic-history courses through this combination.

concepts.label: Social & cultural history
concepts.concept: A social and cultural history programme combines all six UCR History courses with art history, Renaissance connections, African heritage, museums, archaeology and historiography. Social theory, movements, qualitative methods, literature, film, race in media and documentary analysis extend its study of historical experience and representation. Ancient archaeology and literary/media methods supply distinct evidence and perspectives; they do not replace Erasmus’s modern-history and disciplinary-method requirements.
